Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeating: I eat more than usual to distract myself or feel better, Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Hopelessness: I have no future, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Rania was thirty-six when the diagnosis came back: stage three ovarian cancer. She had gone to the clinic with what she thought was indigestion—a heaviness in her abdomen that had worsened over three months—and left with an oncologist's name and a surgery date. The first surgery, in the spring of 2021, revealed how far the disease had spread. Her surgeon used words like "aggressive" and "extensive peritoneal involvement." Rania remembered the surgeon's face as she explained the chemotherapy protocol, the way the woman's eyes softened in a way that felt like pity. That moment—sitting in the examination room with her husband Karim holding her hand, realizing that her body had become a territory she no longer controlled—fractured something in her that had not yet repaired.

The chemotherapy lasted six months. Rania lost her hair, her appetite, her sense of who she was in the world. But she survived. The scans came back clear. She was declared in remission. By all medical measures, she had been given her life back. Yet the life she returned to did not feel like the one she had left. Now, three years later at thirty-nine, Rania felt ancient in her vigilance. Every ache in her body was a harbinger. A twinge in her lower abdomen, a persistent fatigue, a small rash—these were not ordinary discomforts but omens. She had come to believe that her body was fundamentally untrustworthy, that the cancer was still there, waiting, that remission was simply the cancer's patience. What frightened her most was that she could not stop this reasoning, could not convince herself otherwise even when her doctors reassured her with clear scans and normal bloodwork. The fear itself felt like evidence of something true that she alone could perceive.

At the construction firm where she had worked for twelve years, Rania had become someone her colleagues barely recognized. She was a site supervisor—competent, respected—but over the past eighteen months, she had begun arriving earlier and staying later, often working through lunch. She told herself it was about the upcoming residential development, the complexity of the schedule, but the truth was simpler and more desperate: when she was working, her mind could not wander to the territory of her own mortality. At home, she cooked elaborate meals, often making two or three dinners in an evening, eating while she prepared the next one, not tasting any of it. The overeating was automatic, a hand reaching for bread or sweets without conscious decision, her body seeking something that food could never provide. She had gained thirty pounds in two years. When she caught her reflection in the site trailer's window, she sometimes did not recognize herself. The sleep had become nearly impossible. Rania would lie awake beside Karim, her body rigid with tension, convinced that if she relaxed into sleep, something catastrophic would happen—that she would miss a sign, that her body would betray her in the darkness. At three in the morning, she would rise and reorganize the kitchen cupboards or scroll through medical websites, reading about recurrence rates and survival statistics, searching for the logic that would let her feel safe. She startle easily now—a door slamming, a car horn outside—and her nervous system responds as though danger is imminent. Her jaw is perpetually clenched. Her shoulders live at her ears.

The worst part, the thought that had begun to consume her in recent weeks, was that her mind was fracturing under the weight of this vigilance. The way she could not stop catastrophizing, the way she ate without hunger, the way she threw herself into work as though productivity were a shield against death—these patterns frightened her. She wondered if she was losing her grip on reality, if her constant fear meant she was going crazy. She had no future that felt real to her, only an endless present of waiting for the other shoe to drop. Her concentration at work had begun to slip; she had missed details on blueprints twice in the last month, things that would have been unthinkable before. Karim had gently suggested therapy several times. Last week, Rania finally agreed. She sat in the waiting room of the clinic, her hands trembling slightly, hoping that someone could help her understand why surviving felt so much like drowning.
